docs.text: The glacial ancestor of Lake Michigan once drained into Lake Huron much like Erie now drains into Ontario: via a river that topples over a waterfall. The falls are still there, submerged under 150 feet of water just east of Mackinac Island.

Some are more connected than others. Michigan and Huron, which are only separated by the Strait of Mackinac, are basically the same lake hydrologically. Huron and Erie are separated by a series of rivers and Lake St. Claire, and Erie and Ontario are separated by the Niagara River and Falls.

It’s SOME. Huron and Michigan are limnologically one lake. (Since Lake Michigan is entirely surrounded by the US Canadians consider Huron to be the name of the lake, so they use HOSE. That’s how they got to being called “hosers.”)

We get upstream connections to Lake Huron and Lake Michigan fairly often (with a W to NW flow you can get a Michigan connection farther west and a Huron connection farther east at the same time), but we haven’t seen a good/prolonged Huron connection into the Cleveland area in a while.

A geologist come up to me with tears in his eyes and said “sir, these two lakes really should be called the same.” So I think that’s something we’ll do.

Lake Michigan and Lake Huron are hydrologically the same body of water. The Straits of Mackinac act like a natural bridge, letting water flow freely between them, so changes in water level on one lake affect the other almost immediately.
